subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION OF EDUCATIONAL FILMS TO SCHOOL BOARDS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION OF EDUCATIONAL FILMS TO SCHOOL BOARDS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is disappointing that the minister is not here to answer questions on such an important subject. The subject of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation providing educational films to school boards and universities throughout Canada is of major importance and one on which I hope the government can throw some light tonight.
There are certain problems with the present Copyright Act. First, it affects the availability of teaching and learning materials, both print and nonprint. Second, it affects the interests of teachers as participants in the production of educational material. Teachers are prohibited by the present act from fully realizing the potential of the technology available to them and to their students. Third, an example of the copyright problem is that the CBC may hire an outside company to produce an educational film; however, the company may restrict showing rights to the CBC alone and retain the copyright to sell to other institutions. In such a case the CBC is unable to authorize any province or school board to reproduce it.
Another example would be the CBC producing an educational film itself and inserting still photographs belonging to another organization. Again, the permission is limited to use by the CBC. Further difficulties arise when the CBC uses a Hollywood produced film. In a case such as this, the screen actors guild and other organizations may have a claim for unauthorized use.
Adjournment Debate
The following are suggestions for amendments to the present act: (1) copying and duplicating should be allowed for, subject to suitable safeguards to protect the legitimate interests of the creator and publisher; (2) in the case of broadcast programs of an educational nature there should be recognition of the need to record them for playback within a limited period. In this situation the tape recording may be used to meet timetabling requirements without royalty payment; (3) transmission of copyright material through closed-circuit television systems should be subject to reasonable royalties and fees in terms of the specific target audience.
School boards and teachers have experienced distress in recent months because of current inadequacy in legislation and failure to reach agreement at the federal level. The Canadian Teachers' Federation has presented a number of briefs in this regard and I believe note should be made of some of the comments which have been made public. One is as follows:
Since there appears to be widespread expectation that the Copyright Act will be substantially revised in the near future, CTF believes that such a revision should not be long delayed and that it is of the utmost importance that all interested parties should have the opportunity to participate in the revision ... The brief complains that CBC program materials are being handed over to an American-dominated private company for distribution on a profitmaking basis.
Here is a quotation from a statement by Mr. Wendell Sparkes, the CTF president:
I am pleased to have a strong mandate to secure the full and free use in Canadian schools of educational programs developed with the support of public moneys . . . We will present our views regarding the difficulties being experienced with video taping of school telecasts for viewing at a more convenient time because of the present copyright laws as well as certain contractual arrangements at the CBC.
At this point I believe I should bring to light the objections raised by educationalists that though the CBC can obtain complete distribution rights for schools, its commercial outlet, Visual Education Centre, Inc., charges the full commercial rates. An example of this is the handling of the film on smoking entitled "One Way to Quit," a film which I maintain should be made available to students both in high school and in university. This is only one of many possible examples.
It seems unreasonable that productions financed entirely at the expense of the Canadian public should be sold to schools at full commercial rates. The CBC argues, in support of its position, that school boards do not receive free electricity, free telephone service or free mail service from the federal government. I do not believe this is a valid objection when it comes to providing films for use in our schools.
I am in receipt of a letter from the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) informing me that the majority of CBC programs are not accessible to school boards because nontelevision educational rights in most programs broadcast by the corporation either cannot be acquired or do not exist. The minister stated;
This leaves, of course, a number of other programs produced by or for the CBC which may have some value for further use in the classroom. Included among these are the school broadcasts pro-
26635-6!

October 15, 1973
Adjournment Debate
duced in co-operation with the Council of Ministers of Education and with provincial departments of education. CBC has been giving this program serious study over the past several months. This includes a detailed review of the cost and implications of releasing programs, where possible, for school and other uses, the suitability and adaptability of collective agreements with the talent unions, the possible impact on CBC administration and on the private non-theatrical film production and distribution industries.
The minister further stated:
The CBC is conscious of the desirability of making an early statement on the matter of providing some programs for use in schools.
In closing, let me say this. I feel many newscasts could be made more readily available. At present they can only be shown once. Series about certain countries cannot be reshown. Surely no royalties have to be paid to CBC announcers, or animals appearing in films.
The government and the CBC have had more than a reasonable amount of time in which to provide solutions to these problems. Answers are long overdue. School boards, school trustees, teachers, university administrators and members of parliament in all parties have patiently waited for some action to be taken by the minister. It is the hope of thousands of citizens across this nation that the hon. gentleman will provide a positive and firm commitment tonight with respect to providing educational and other films to our educational institutions.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-APPEAL AGAINST DECISION CONDEMNING RED CIRCLING-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF PRACTICE AND APPROPRIATE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 18 of this year, as reported at page 6672 of Hansard, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) whether the government was considering appealing the decision of Professor Abbott in which he condemned the practice of red circling in the well known Morency case. It was asked in the hope that the Government of Canada would see just what hardship this practice has brought about and that the government would at the same time put an end to it once and for all. My hopes were in vain, but in view of this government's record I ought not to have been surprised that it would do nothing in this particular case. In fact, a few days ago an announcement was made that the appeal was being launched. I regret the decision and that action and the attitude toward the public service which is evidenced by it.
I asked the question and I asked for this debate because I know of no practice in the public service that is more contrary to the principle of the merit system. There is no doubt that Professor Abbott's decision is a benchmark on the road to real justice for public servants, and as such it ought to have been allowed to stand. I will make no comment on whether or not the appeal launched by the government has any status in law because of delay, for that may well be a matter of law to be argued before the next tribunal and possibly before the courts. But that consideration ought not to detract from the importance of the decision in the working life of public servants.
Aside from the moral issue involved-and in my submission the balance in respect of the moral issue is on the side of the public servant-it is my contention that the process of red circling is unlawful, and this view is strengthened by the judgment of Professor Abbott. The Public Service Alliance of Canada has argued consistently, with great force, that an employee can be demoted only if it is shown that he is very incompetent or incapable. There is no authority in law for demotion on any other basis.
In this case the employer took the view that it had the unqualified right to classify and reclassify jobs or add or detract from duties, and when reclassification is to a lower level the employer also had the right to place the employee concerned in a holding scale of rates. The employer also took the position that when the salary of a CR-4 reached Mr. Morency's CR-5 salary, the employer had the right to demote Mr. Morency from CR-5 to CR-4 for no reason other than the fact that his position had been reclassified downward as a result of departmental reorganization.
October 15, 1973

There is no argument that the government or the employer has the right to reclassify. I do not think there is any argument that the government has the right to change the duties assigned to any person if it chooses to do so, at least as the law stands now. However, I want to quote from the brief filed by the PSAC in respect of the position taken by the government as follows:
What we do not agree with is that an employee can be deprived of any further salary increases because the employer has exercised its right to downgrade the level of the position which he encumbers. If the employer was right, if it can forestall any salary increase simply by reducing the level of positions in the public service, then collective bargaining would be a nullity. If we obtained through arbitration a salary increase for the CR group which was higher than that which the employer wished to pay, all the employer would have to do is reclassify all CR positions downward by one grade and then, rather than gaining any increases in salary, all employees in the group would be red circled and eventually demoted. Just to state that proposition is sufficient. It is obviously ridiculous.
To that I should like to add that it is patently unjust. Then the brief went on to deal with another matter, and it said this:
Under section 10 of the Employment Act, the law requires that all "appointments to or from within the public service shall be based on selection according to merit, as determined by the commission . .."
Mr. Speaker, the actions of the government from the beginning of the Morency case flew in the face of the merit principle. The Abbott judgment states that the principle of justice cannot be ignored. The government ought to reconsider its position, admit it has been wrong and avoid further delay through this costly appeal procedure in the face of a good judgment, the cost of the delay and the many public servants affected by the judgment.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-APPEAL AGAINST DECISION CONDEMNING RED CIRCLING-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF PRACTICE AND APPROPRIATE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with some interest to the hon. member's rhetoric. I almost said "oratory," but "rhetoric" is a much better term. The hon. gentleman said that red circling is the equivalent of demotion, and that the Public Service Act contemplates a formal procedure for demotion which can be carried out only on the grounds of incompetence or other specific reasons. I would point out that his understanding of the process known as red circling must be imperfect if he attributes any method of demotion to red circling. In fact he has said-and I quote from the
Adjournment Debate
brief of his informant-that the government has and must continue to have the right to reassign duties and reclassify jobs, not people, in the public service. This it does.
In the process of reorganization, or reclassification and of the reassignment of duties there will be occasions in which the nature of the duties of a man or woman has changed, perhaps in the sense of becoming less onerous and less responsible, in which case that particular job will carry a lower classification on review than it did previously when the duties were different. When this happens, rather than impose a financial penalty on the public servant, provision is made that he will continue at his existing salary for his old classification or his or her old grade and will continue to get the normal annual increases provided for that salary range. However, he or she will not get the negotiated changes for the old classification which is no longer appropriate, but there will be no loss or diminution of salary, and in this sense no demotion. The job has been changed and perhaps it has been downgraded.
The hon. gentleman acknowledged the right of the government to redistribute duties. The civil servant has not been demoted; he continues to enjoy the same salary, and I am glad to say that the concern of the department and of the Public Service Commission has been to endeavour assiduously to find elsewhere appropriate work carrying the man's original classification. It is only in cases where it is not possible to effect a transfer to the original classification, or in some cases where the individual does not wish to move, that the red circling process comes into operation.
Given the right of the government in the execution of its duties to the taxpayers to reorganize departments, to reclassify positions, I consider this, rather than being unjust to be a very fair and very just system to ensure that those who are overtaken by changes in operational functions do not suffer financial penalty.
I should point out in closing that the converse of red circling is green circling. No one complains that when the nature of a job has been changed and its classification is discovered to be too low, there is no hesitancy or unwillingness on the part of either the government or the employee to raise the remuneration for that position.
